source.title: Triple descent in quantum linear regression
source.authors: Gabriele Lo Monaco; Salvatore Lorenzo; A. Ferraro; M. Paternostro; G. Palma; Luca Innocenti

page_placements.theme: Overparameterization and feature noise as implicit ridge regularization

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes double- and triple-descent behavior with a different method and in quantum linear regression, including its dependence on measurement outcomes, training-set size, shot noise, and ridge regularization.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own analytical results and simulations. Results cited from other work and schematic figures are not recorded as findings. Training-shot counts and ridge settings are recorded only as conditions, not as outcomes.
record.test_reason: New setting: quantum linear regression with finite-shot features. Analytic theorems and simulations show test variance and MSE peaks at interpolation thresholds as outcome count or training-set size varies. They also show how these peaks depend on shot noise and ridge, bearing on V3, V4 and V6. T3 fits better than T2: the question is posed in a new model class, not answered with a new method on the original setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct; it needs these additions. The quantum peak is not removed by more training or test shots and vanishes only with exactly known training features (the limits N→∞ and N=∞ do not commute). The classical peak persists with exact features but is suppressed by low training-shot budgets and by more test shots. Ridge makes the peak finite, with height ∝η^−1/2, and the optimal strength depends on both shot budgets.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes quantum linear regression with finite-shot measurement probabilities, random POVMs, and random-matrix theory; it does not reproduce the original deep-network model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The classical peak is suppressed at lower training-shot budgets. The quantum peak depends on training-shot precision, persists at fixed dimension as training shots increase, and is absent with exact training features. Positive ridge rounds the peak, and the ridge strength minimizing MSE depends on test-shot budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing training shots N strengthens the test-variance peak amplitude (CV rises toward 1) and saturates it at fixed d. The ideal-test amplitude falls as 1/α. Fig. 9 and Fig. 10(a); eqs. (22)-(23).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More measurement precision on training features (shots, not samples) can raise the test-variance interpolation peak.

fits_no_version.finding: Low training-shot budgets suppress the classical peak at nout=d², acting as an effective ridge with τN=1/(N nout). Fig. 5 and Fig. 8.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature noise can act as implicit regularization that removes one descent peak.

record.problems: The central claims concern quantum linear regression, not deep networks. The main asymptotic peak results rely on proportional high-dimensional limits and stated geometric and trace assumptions; finite-dimensional peaks fluctuate across measurements and training records. Some plotted evidence is summarized qualitatively in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result bearing on the tested claim versions was omitted.

untested.parts: No deep networks; model size of neural networks not varied.
Only quantum linear regression. The claim that the curve subsumes a classical U-shaped regime is not examined.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed. Peaks sit at two distinct thresholds (nout=d², nout=ntr) set by different mechanisms.
Label-noise-driven peak at ntr=d² is only described schematically (Fig. 2), not computed or simulated. Optimal-regularization elimination is not directly tested.
Tested only for test variance and ideal-test error as ntr crosses nout; not in deep networks or standard label-noise settings.

missing.what: Classical variance peak at nout=d² for N=16 to 10⁸, d=8: sharp at large N, progressively flattened at low N (noise-induced suppression).
Below-IC interpolation peak (nout=32<d²) as ntr crosses interpolation: present with exact features, lowered but not removed by finite shots; Theorem 5.
Training-shot dependence at interpolation (N=16 to 4^10). The variance peak saturates as N grows at fixed d, while ideal-test error decreases.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The reader's V6 label listed R5/R6, which are unlinked to V6; they were removed. Most results are asymptotic theorems, with medians from simulations shown in figures; few exact numbers are read off in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model size is not varied.
Training epochs or time are not varied.
The study tests training-set size near the interpolation threshold in its quantum linear-regression setting, not generally across deep networks or other model classes.
The study tests variation in measurement-outcome count in quantum linear regression; it does not establish the curve across model classes generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study examines measurement shot noise and ridge regularization, but does not establish that an optimally tuned regularizer eliminates the peaks in general.
The study does not test whether a suitable effective-parameter count converts second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Quantum linear regression with Haar-random rank-one POVMs
rows.size_stated: Hilbert-space dimension d; measurement outcomes nout
rows.operation_detail: Analytically vary the number of measurement outcomes with exact training probabilities and measure test variance.
rows.measure: Target- and Haar-test-state-averaged test variance, normalized by d∆²O
rows.value: For γC = d²/nout ≠ 1, the limiting normalized variance is min{1, γC⁻¹}/|1 − γC|; at γC = 1 (nout = d²), it diverges in probability.
rows.uncertainty: Convergence in probability as d → ∞; no numerical error bar stated for the theorem.
rows.note: This is the classical measurement-frame peak. The study says it persists with exact training probabilities and is suppressed by more test shots when considering its contribution to prediction error.
rows.check: Analytic, noise-free training (exact frame, Vex). The peak at nout=d² arises from measurement-frame ill-conditioning amplifying test-shot variance, not from label noise. For V6 it supports 'variance-driven', not 'label-noise-driven'.

rows.subject: Quantum linear regression above informational completeness
rows.size_stated: nout and ntr proportional to d²
rows.operation_detail: Vary outcome count relative to training-state count at finite training-shot precision and measure test variance.
rows.measure: Target-averaged test variance, normalized by d∆²O
rows.value: As nout/ntr → 1, the ridgeless test variance diverges in probability; the median diverges. The study identifies this as the quantum interpolation peak.
rows.uncertainty: Convergence in probability; finite-size distributions are shown in Fig. 6 with median, 95% confidence intervals, and percentile ranges.
rows.locator: Section IV B, Theorem 3; Section IV, Fig. 6
rows.note: The theorem includes rank-deficient measured feature matrices. The study attributes the peak to finite-shot fluctuations populating outcome directions absent from exact Born probabilities.

source_check.locator_found: Section IV B, Theorem 3, equation (18), and Figure 6.

rows.subject: Quantum linear regression above informational completeness
rows.size_stated: nout and ntr proportional to d²
rows.operation_detail: Analyze finite-shot prediction-error profiles near the interpolation ratio under positive ridge regularization.
rows.baseline: Ridgeless profile has a 1/|γ − 1| singularity near interpolation.
rows.value: Near γ = 1, Fη(γ) is asymptotic to CV/√((γ − 1)² + 4hη); at γ = 1 its height grows as CV/√(2hη) as ridge weakens.
rows.uncertainty: Asymptotic result under stated empirical bounds and critical trace regularity; no numerical error bar stated for the theorem.
rows.note: Positive ridge rounds the divergence to a finite peak; the result does not say that the peak disappears.
rows.check: Asymptotic theorem. Ridge turns the 1/|γ−1| pole into a finite peak of height ∝η^−1/2; it does not remove the peak.

source_check.locator_found: Section IV B, Theorem 4, equation (19); Section IV D, equation (24).

rows.subject: Quantum linear regression, d = 4
rows.operation_detail: Vary nout across the informational-completeness and interpolation thresholds and measure full test MSE.
rows.value: The study reports that decreasing N strongly rounds the first peak while the interpolation peak remains pronounced.
rows.uncertainty: Medians over 1024 realizations; shading shows 10th–90th percentiles and error bars pointwise 95% confidence intervals for the median.
rows.note: The reported curve has two peaks as nout crosses the two thresholds, giving the triple-descent profile.

source_check.locator_found: Section IV C, Figure 8 and caption.

rows.subject: Quantum linear regression, d = 12
rows.operation_detail: Vary ntr across interpolation and report test variance.
rows.value: The profile has a peak near nout = ntr; positive ridge rounds it.
rows.uncertainty: 128 independent realizations per point; medians and pointwise 10th–90th percentiles shown.
rows.note: With nout fixed, increasing ntr moves the ratio through interpolation; the peak therefore indicates a setting where adding training states raises test variance.
rows.check: The ridge-rounding part bears on V6 but is already covered by R3/R7. Drop R5 from the V6 label rather than relinking it. Measure is test variance only.

source_check.locator_found: Section IV B, Figure 7(a) and caption.

rows.subject: Quantum linear regression, d = 12
rows.operation_detail: Vary ntr across interpolation and report ideal-test error.
rows.value: The profile peaks near nout = ntr; positive ridge rounds the peak.
rows.uncertainty: 128 independent realizations per point; medians and pointwise 10th–90th percentiles shown.
rows.note: The study reports this as error in reconstructing the learned observable, which persists with exact test probabilities.
rows.check: Same as R5. The V6 label cited R5/R6 though neither row is linked to V6; remove them from that label.

source_check.locator_found: Section IV B, Figure 7(b) and caption; Section II B, equation (6).

rows.subject: Quantum linear regression at interpolation
rows.operation_detail: Compare prediction-error costs across ridge strengths and test-shot budgets.
rows.value: Increasing ridge first reduces MSE and then increases it by attenuating the target signal; the minimum depends on M.
rows.uncertainty: 1024 Haar and multinomial realizations; medians and 10th–90th percentiles shown.
rows.note: A ridge choice can reduce the peak, but the study reports a trade-off and does not report that tuning makes the peak disappear.
rows.check: MSE at interpolation has an interior ridge optimum that depends on M. No statement that tuned ridge removes the peak relative to neighbouring nout.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V6 peak elimination. At fixed nout=ntr=1024, increasing ridge first decreases and then increases MSE; the minimizing displayed ridge depends on M. This does not determine whether an optimally regularized complexity curve retains a peak.

source_check.notes: The effective-ridge interpretation uses approximately balanced measurements and concentration when ntr is much larger than nout; it fails near interpolation. Theorem 2 concerns reference weights from the exact POVM; below informational completeness, finite-sample exact-feature regression need not return those weights.

statements.correction: Positive ridge produces finite interpolation peaks; their small-ridge heights scale as eta^(-1/2). Figure 11(c) finds M-dependent MSE minima at fixed interpolation. Elimination of peaks under optimal tuning is untested; these results do not supply an against verdict on that claim.
statements.problem: The quantum-regression facts are correct, but the limits_scope classification relies on an untested optimal-regularization claim.
